answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the logical "Cosmos DB account" resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in 'az cosmosdb' command group. Example to create: az cosmosdb create -n myAccount -g myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. This is in the core az CLI (not a third-party extension).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (for the account) and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for DB/collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Scheme: mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// (MongoDB drivers). Host suffix for Cosmos Mongo API: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or SRV entry on that domain). TLS/SSL port commonly 10255 for non-SRV TLS connections. Typical example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/myDatabase?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Use tls/ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false in the query string for Cosmos Mongo API connections.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units per second, RU/s) with options for provisioned throughput and autoscale. There is also a serverless option for some Cosmos workloads; there is not a simple vCore tier for the classic Mongo API accounts (billing is RU-based).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary supported auth for the MongoDB API is MongoDB-style user/password (SCRAM) using the account keys or database users in the account. Management/management-plane operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra). There is no widely used out-of-the-box flow where a MongoDB driver directly performs AAD/OAuth authentication against the Mongo endpoint; drivers typically connect with username/password in the connection string. (If AAD-to-Mongo auth is required it would be a special integration and is not the default.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the official MongoDB Node.js driver) and Mongoose for Node.js. There is not a separate "DocumentDB Mongo" driver; the service implements the MongoDB wire protocol so use the official Mongo/Mongoose client libraries.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: I expect support for common vector index types such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN on vector-capable clusters. A Mongo-like createIndex command would look like: db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vectorIndexType: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dimensions: 1536, 'hnswOptions': { M:16, efConstruction:200 } }). (This is my best practical guess at the index options/syntax.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is typically handled by integrating Azure Cognitive Search (or another search engine) over Cosmos DB data; for hybrid text+vector search you either use a search service that supports both (Azure Cognitive Search with vector support) or you perform vector nearest-neighbour queries in the DB and combine results with text scoring in the application or an external search layer. The MongoDB API itself does not provide Atlas Search; use an Azure search layer for advanced text or hybrid search.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports specific MongoDB server versions/wire protocol levels (customers typically choose a server-version compatibility like 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4/5.0/6.0/7.0 depending on account). Some advanced MongoDB features may be limited or not supported (server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages or filesystem features, cross-partition multi-document transactions with scale limitations, and certain admin commands). Verify supported server-version for your account before using cutting-edge MongoDB features.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: For local development use the official MongoDB Docker image (for the matching Mongo server version you target, e.g. mongo:7). The Mongo default port is 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists for Windows (and now has a Linux container variant) but it historically does not fully emulate every Mongo API feature—so for Mongo-specific development run a local mongo container: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are available on many Cosmos DB Mongo API compatibility versions. In many accounts you can use the MongoDB changeStream API (collection.watch()). There may be account/version prerequisites; in general nothing extra in-app must be enabled beyond using a compatible API version, but check the account's supported features if change streams are critical.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile (the service-specific MCP server) to access data-plane inspection tools for DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo API. The general Azure MCP server covers management-plane operations, but the 'documentdb' MCP server gives more targeted data-plane commands and inspectors for this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service called Azure DocumentDB (the JSON document DB) which evolved and was renamed into Azure Cosmos DB. "DocumentDB" as the old name is part of that history. Azure Cosmos DB exposes multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible API. The unrelated open-source 'DocumentDB' (if you mean other projects) is not the same as Microsoft's old service—Microsoft's DocumentDB became Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is the Azure Cosmos DB service which implements the MongoDB wire protocol (a translation layer) rather than running upstream mongod behind the scenes for all accounts. That means you should use MongoDB drivers, but expect some behavioral and feature differences (aggregation / transactions / server-side features) compared with a stock MongoDB server; code that uses basic CRUD, indexes and common aggregations will usually work unchanged.

answers.question: What database name will this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named 'sample_retail_10' for all collections and operations in this sample.

answers.question: How will the sample read the cluster connection string from the environment?
answers.answer: Read the Mongo connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime (process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI in Node.js) and pass that to mongoose.connect(). Do not hard-code or log the value.

answers.question: What index definitions does this sample need to create for tenant isolation and query performance?
answers.answer: Create compound indexes: 1) db.products.createIndex({ tenantId: 1, sku: 1 }, { name: 'tenant_sku_idx' }) (sku unique per tenant if desired, make it unique: { unique: true }). 2) db.orders.createIndex({ tenantId: 1, createdAt: -1 }, { name: 'tenant_createdAt_idx' }). Apply the same pattern for inventory: db.inventory.createIndex({ tenantId: 1, sku: 1 }).

answers.question: How will tenant isolation be enforced in the repository layer?
answers.answer: Enforce tenant isolation by requiring tenantId as an explicit parameter for all repository methods and by always adding { tenantId } into the query filters before calling Mongoose/driver methods. Additionally register Mongoose query middleware (pre 'find'/'findOne'/'update' hooks) to assert tenantId presence or automatically inject a tenantId filter, so no repository method can return or modify documents across tenants.

answers.question: What TLS/connection options will the sample require when connecting to the live cluster?
answers.answer: Require TLS: ensure the connection string includes tls/ssl=true (or use mongodb+srv which implies TLS). For Cosmos Mongo API include replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false if needed. The sample will not disable TLS and will not connect without the DOCUMENTDB_URI containing the proper TLS options.
